headline: Bolsonaro finishes first as Brazil heads to a runoff

sources.title: Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula-Bolsonaro runoff as right gains ground (NPR, via WUNC)
Brazil's presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round (Al Jazeera)
Brazil heads to run-off as Flávio Bolsonaro takes first place finish over Lula (Buenos Aires Times / AFP)
Brazil vote set for runoff as Flavio Bolsonaro sees surprise lead (video, Reuters)

chunks.text: Brazil held the [[first round]] of its presidential election on October 4, 2026. Senator Bolsonaro {{came in}} first with about 47 percent of the vote. President Lula got about 45 percent. A candidate needs more than half the valid votes to win [[outright]]. Both men {{fell short of}} that [[mark]]. Lula will now {{take on}} Bolsonaro in a runoff on October 25. The result shows a country [[evenly split]] between two leaders.

verbs.correct: To finish a race at a given place
verbs.wrong: To make a speech to voters
verbs.why: Our team came in second at the state finals. She came in third in the race last year. Senator Bolsonaro came in first with about 47 percent of the vote.

verbs.correct: To fail to reach a goal or level
verbs.wrong: To leave a race before the end
verbs.why: The school fell short of its goal of 500 books. His test score fell short of what he needed. Both men fell short of the more than half of the votes needed to win.
Our team will take on the champions on Friday. She plans to take on the mayor in next year's race. Lula will take on Bolsonaro in a runoff on October 25.

chunks.text: The result {{turned out}} differently from what most [[opinion polls]] had shown. Most of them had put Lula in first place. Bolsonaro {{racked up}} about 56 million votes. That is more than his father, a former president, received in 2018 or 2022. The candidates who finished third, fourth and fifth are all [[right-wing]]. Two right-wing candidates won about 5.3 million votes together. Both have said they will not [[endorse]] either man in the runoff.

verbs.wrong: To be counted a second time
verbs.why: The party turned out better than we planned. Her first day at work turned out fine. The result turned out differently from what most opinion polls had shown.

verbs.wrong: To promise votes to a party
verbs.why: The singer racked up ten awards in one night. He racked up a lot of points in the game. Bolsonaro racked up about 56 million votes in the first round.

chunks.text: Brazilians also elected members of Congress. Right-wing parties did well in both [[chambers]] and {{picked up}} [[seats]] in the Senate. Bolsonaro's party was [[on track]] to become the largest group in the [[lower house]]. A stronger right could make it harder for Lula to {{get his plans through}} Congress. Bolsonaro has promised to {{carry on}} his father's [[legacy]]. His father is serving a 27-year [[prison sentence]] for [[plotting]] to [[overturn]] his 2022 election loss to Lula.

verbs.why: The team picked up three more points on Sunday. Her party picked up two seats on the city council. Right-wing parties picked up seats in the Senate.

verbs.correct: To have a plan approved by lawmakers
verbs.wrong: To write a plan for new laws
verbs.why: The mayor could not get the new tax through the city council. She finally got her school plan through the state Senate. A stronger right could make it harder for Lula to get his plans through Congress.

verbs.correct: To continue what someone else started
verbs.wrong: To win more votes than a rival
verbs.why: She wants to carry on her mother's work at the bakery. The new coach will carry on the old coach's training plan. Bolsonaro has promised to carry on his father's legacy.

chunks.text: Bolsonaro, who is 45, says Brazil wants change. He has also promised to {{bring down}} the [[budget deficit]]. Lula, who is 80, is seeking a fourth term. Analysts say that to {{hold on to}} power he must {{win back}} younger voters who supported him in 2022. He has promised to {{stand up to}} US pressure on Latin America. A Bolsonaro win would add to a [[wave]] of right-wing victories across the region.

verbs.why: The city wants to bring down the cost of bus tickets. Exercise can help bring down your blood pressure. Bolsonaro has promised to bring down the budget deficit.

verbs.correct: To keep something you already have
verbs.wrong: To let a court make a decision
verbs.why: The team held on to first place all season. The mayor hopes to hold on to her job in the next election. Analysts say Lula must win back younger voters to hold on to power.

verbs.correct: To regain the support of people
verbs.wrong: To count people in a survey
verbs.why: The store lowered its prices to win back customers. He apologized to win back his friends. Analysts say Lula needs to win back younger voters who supported him in 2022.

verbs.correct: To resist pressure from someone stronger
verbs.wrong: To seek help from a stronger country
verbs.why: She stood up to the boss who treated her badly. Small towns sometimes stand up to big companies. Lula has promised to stand up to US pressure on Latin America.

wordDefs.def: Likely to reach a goal or result

ex: The higher court may overturn the judge's decision.

wordDefs.def: The amount by which a government spends more than it earns
ex: The state has a large budget deficit this year.
Higher taxes could help close the budget deficit.

wordDefs.def: A large number of similar events that happen in a short time
ex: The city saw a wave of new restaurants open last year.

mainIdea.s: Brazil's presidential race goes to a second round after neither top candidate won more than half the votes. The right also did well in Congress, which could shape Brazil and the region.
mainIdea.why: Both men fell short of the votes needed to win outright, so there will be a runoff on October 25. Right-wing parties also picked up seats in the Senate.

mainIdea.s: Bolsonaro won the first round after two other right-wing candidates asked their supporters to vote for him. Both of these rivals now plan to campaign at his side until October 25.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the two right-wing candidates who were knocked out have said they will not endorse either man in the runoff.

mainIdea.s: Brazil's Congress has passed a new law that makes voting optional for all adults. Supporters say this change will save money, but critics fear that fewer young people will take part.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the first round of Brazil's presidential election. Lula will take on Bolsonaro in a runoff on October 25.

lines.text: Did you see the results from Brazil's election?
I heard it's going to a runoff. Who {{came in}} first?
Senator Bolsonaro, with about 47 percent. He {{racked up}} about 56 million votes.
And Lula got about 45? Wow, that's [[too close to call]].
And it {{turned out}} differently from the polls. Most of them had Lula in first place.
So both of them {{fell short of}} half the votes?
Right. Now Lula has to {{take on}} Bolsonaro in a runoff on October 25.
It sounds like the country is [[split down the middle]].
It is. The right also {{picked up}} seats in the Senate.
That could make it harder for Lula to {{get his plans through}}.
Only if he wins. Nothing is [[a sure thing]] yet.
He says he'll {{carry on}} his father's legacy and {{bring down}} the deficit.
Analysts say he has to {{win back}} younger voters to {{hold on to}} power.
Well, [[at the end of the day]], the voters will decide.
True. In a race this close, [[every vote counts]].

expressions.def: Used to say that nobody can tell yet who will win
ex: The game was too close to call until the last minute.
News channels said the race for mayor was too close to call.

expressions.def: Used to say that a group is divided into two equal halves
ex: My family is split down the middle on pizza toppings.

expressions.def: Something that is certain to happen or succeed
ex: The new job isn't a sure thing yet.
Everyone said the team was a sure thing, but it lost.

expressions.expr: at the end of the day
expressions.def: Used to give the most important point after thinking about everything
ex: At the end of the day, you have to make your own choice.

expressions.def: Used to say that each single vote can change the result
ex: The last election was decided by ten votes, so every vote counts.
